pdf.title: When can a standby issue tickets?

sections.heading: The ticket desk
sections.body: Five replicas issue one-use loading tickets. A front desk accepts a request with token u, proposes (u, lane) and waits for three signed acknowledgments before handing the driver a receipt. The standby desk can take over after reading three replica journals. A driver can visit a second desk before a delayed response from the first desk arrives. Every replica compares tokens by byte equality. A newer election term alone does not invalidate an already issued receipt.

sections.heading: Exercise 1 · One-term snapshots
sections.body: Mark which three journals a takeover might read before delivery of the acknowledgment from c. Give both the visible prefix and the longest prefix that must have been acknowledged by a quorum. Explain why the shortest journal cannot by itself disprove the existence of a receipt. In your table, distinguish a read response from a row whose value is inferred only by quorum intersection.

sections.heading: Exercise 2 · Recovery argument
sections.body: Now let the first desk crash immediately after it sends a receipt. The standby proposes a lane change for the same token. Write an invariant that says a driver with a durable receipt cannot later observe a distinct authorized lane for that token. Enumerate the transition that creates a receipt, the transition that elects a desk, and the transition that discards a reused token. Either prove each preserves the invariant or construct one message interleaving that violates it. Include the earliest inconsistent pair of records.

sections.heading: A tempting optimization
sections.body: A teammate keeps only the greatest scalar high-water mark from the three recovery replies. Test this proposal by varying the token assignments while keeping the returned marks unchanged. Provide a pair of executions if the optimization loses information. Your solution may assume authentic signatures; it may not use clock order between replicas. Submit the trace and a paragraph naming the state that must survive a reboot.

pdf.title: Can a bridge retire its old route?

sections.heading: System and failure model
sections.body:
A control process C moves a stream from bridge A to bridge B. Producers attach a monotonically increasing sequence number and a generation to each packet. A producer may retransmit after a timeout. The network may reorder, duplicate and delay packets, including acknowledgments. Channels do not fabricate messages. There is one producer for each stream and at most one controller is active at any moment. Do not assume synchronized clocks or FIFO delivery.
    
The producer's log and the controller's durable record survive a crash. A bridge loses its in-memory deduplication map on restart. Each bridge has a stable disk journal for effects it has already applied. The controller may crash between sending a message and appending a record. Each handler invocation is atomic, but a handler and a disk append at another process are separate events.

sections.heading: Part A · Reconstruct one execution
sections.body: Reconstruct both the controller's durable state and the externally visible effects after every event. Write the generation attached to each acknowledgment. If information is missing, list the legal possibilities. For the replay sheet, a short table is sufficient. Do not silently drop a duplicate to make the timeline consistent.

rows: Send (stream s, g=7, seq=18) to A.
Journal the effect for seq=18. Send ACK; delivery stalls.
Write closing(7,18). Send DRAIN(7,18) to A.
Deliver an older ACK for seq=17, g=7 to C.
A restarts. C receives a DRAINED message for generation 6.
Timeout for seq=18; retry under the old generation.

sections.heading: Protocol supplied for analysis
sections.body: Every message includes stream, generation and sequence number, except DRAINED, which includes only stream and generation. The stable cursor last[g] is the largest contiguous effect journaled for g. durable_mode and cutoff are colocated. Append-before-send ordering matters. The shorthand emit() makes the new route visible to the producer. The last line below runs only on controller recovery.
sections.code:
on switch(s,k): persist(closing(g,k)); send DRAIN(s,g,k) to A
A.on DRAIN(s,g,k): if last[g] >= k: send DRAINED(s,g) to C
C.on DRAINED(s,x): if durable_mode == closing: emit(OPEN(s,g+1))
C.recover(): if durable_mode == closing: resend DRAIN(s,g,cutoff)

sections.heading: Part B · Safety proof or legal counterexample
sections.body:
No effect from a packet admitted on the retiring route may be lost when the new route becomes visible. State precisely which packets count as admitted. Decide whether the supplied protocol enforces this property across crash and replay. If your answer is yes, give a quantified invariant, establish initialization and address every handler that changes it. If no, give the shortest trace you can justify. Identify the first event after which the property can no longer be guaranteed.

Analyze a delayed DRAINED for a different generation and a crash after emit but before the next stable record separately. State any additional stable information a repaired protocol needs. Show why matching a generation alone does or does not suffice when the producer retries an already journaled effect. An argument that depends on eventual delivery must identify the step at which it uses that assumption.

sections.heading: What to hand in
sections.body: Submit a state table for A and a separate argument for B. Use event numbers when referring to the replay. For the repair, include the changed guard or write order and one adversarial execution it rules out. We grade a counterexample on whether every message in it can arise under the stated handlers. Diagrams and pseudocode are welcome when accompanied by a written claim explaining what the diagram establishes.
